title: In 1957 the Sydney Opera House was budgeted at A$7 million.
description:
In 1957 the Sydney Opera House was budgeted at A$7 million. That was 3.5 million pounds. The planned completion date was 26 January 1963, Australia Day.

The final cost in Australian dollars, nearly fifteen times the estimate. It opened on 20 October 1973, ten years after the planned date.

Utzon never saw it finished. He left the project on 28 February 1966 and never returned to Australia. He was invited to the opening and did not come.

Psychologists call this the planning fallacy. Kahneman and Tversky first proposed it. It is the tendency to underestimate the time, costs and risks of future actions while overestimating the benefits.

A 1994 study of 37 students found the same bias. They predicted 33.9 days on average to finish. The real average was 55.5 days, and only about 30 per cent finished on their predicted date.

Your own deadline is probably optimistic too.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Opera_House: read. Established that 1957 estimates projected a cost of 3,500,000 pounds ($7 million) and completion on 26 January 1963; that the final cost was A$102 million; that Queen Elizabeth II formally opened it on 20 October 1973; that Utzon left the project on 28 February 1966 and left Australia never to return; and that he was in fact invited to the 1973 opening.
- https://www.sydneyoperahouse.com/our-story/utzon-departs-the-house: read. Established that the cost was estimated at just 3.5 million pounds when construction began in 1959, and that Utzon would never return to Australia to see how his building had been completed by others.
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planning_fallacy: read. Established the definition (predictions of time needed show an optimism bias), the Lovallo and Kahneman 2003 wording (underestimating time, costs and risks while overestimating benefits), that Kahneman and Tversky first proposed the idea, that the Opera House is listed as an example, and the Buehler, Griffin and Ross 1994 result of 33.9 days predicted against 55.5 days actual for 37 students, with about 30 per cent finishing on their predicted date.
